Hunting for NSD exploitation attempts instead of waiting for an alert


No public exploit has been reported for the four NSD stack overwrite flaws fixed in 4.15.3, and SecurityOnline records no confirmed in-the-wild use. That absence is a reason to build detection before the code appears, not a reason to relax. The flaws sit in the zone-file parser, which means the interesting events happen around zone loading rather than around DNS queries.
NLnet Labs lists CVE-2026-101338, CVE-2026-101339, CVE-2026-101341 and CVE-2026-101337 as stack overwrites in NSD 4.10.0 through 4.15.2. Each requires a crafted zone file fed directly to the parser. The vendor states that zone files written by NSD itself, as happens for a secondary receiving transfers, will not be formatted the way the attacks require,…

import shutil
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("Downloads")
for f in folder.iterdir():

articles.description:
"Make it look like film" sounds like a texture request. It is really four separate changes to how your pixels behave, and the difference between applying them and just stamping noise on top is the difference between a photo that reads as scanned film and a photo that reads as a filtered phone shot.
Here is what actually changes, and how to tell what a tool did.
Grain sits in the midtones, not everywhere. Organic film grain is strongest in the middle values and nearly invisible in deep shadows and blown highlights, because it is an artifact of dye clouds, not an overlay. A noise layer applied uniformly at a fixed opacity is the single most recognizable tell of a fake: grain over jet-black areas does not happen on real film.
Highlights roll off instead of clipping. Film negative handles over…
articles.title: "Film look" is a contrast curve, not a noise stamp — what style presets actually change

articles.author: Joud Awad
articles.description:
I have seen a lot of engineers think about data one way: how do I store it, and how do I query it?
Data engineers ask something else: where does all this data land, and what can I build from it?
That gap gets wider as your system grows.
5 services means 5 data shapes, 5 formats, 5 update patterns. Reading and writing rows is the least interesting thing you can do with them.
Clean them, join them, and you get product features, stakeholder dashboards, and an honest view of what’s actually happening inside your system.
There are 3 places that data can live:
Data Lake


Data Warehouse



So most teams ran both.
A lake for raw data and ML. A warehouse for BI. Pipelines copying between them. Two copies, two bills, and one of them is always stale.
Data Lakehouse
Keep the data in cheap object storage, in open formats, and put a table layer on top: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, or Hudi.
That layer gives you ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and row-level updates.
One copy of the data. BI and ML read the same tables.
It’s not a new storage system. It’s metadata on top of files you already have.
Weakness: you own more of the operations, like compaction, the small-files problem, and picking a catalog.
Rule of thumb:
I walk through all three in the full video:
https://youtu.be/dRDaQ7wZHTg
Over to you: is your team still running a lake and a warehouse side by side, or have you moved to Iceberg or Delta?
articles.title: Data Lake vs Data Warehouse vs Data Lakehouse: Data Engineering Simplified

Choose Google Cloud Pub/Sub when the team needs more control around subscriptions and can absorb the extra configuration. Keep the reminder itself asynchronous: the scheduler should enqueue work, and a worker should own delivery, retry, and idempotency.
